plan: Six new SAT R&W items aimed at upper difficulty (unwarranted conclusion WIC, persisting inducible defense inference, control-group temperature data, mid-clause however boundary, Maxwell rings replacement transition, tree-ring method synthesis) plus six batch-47 items resubmitted as revision 2 (S047-01 rebuilt as qualified praise; S047-02 adds a marigold-free baseline; S047-03 and S047-05 choice lengths; S047-04 remember length; S047-09 unchanged, flag was an intended lure). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: An inevitable treaty?
passages.text: Although the historian's account of the treaty negotiations is meticulously documented, her conclusion that the agreement was inevitable seems ______, since several of the letters she herself cites show delegates on the verge of abandoning the talks.

passages.title: Spines on demand
passages.text: Some water fleas grow protective spines only when they detect chemicals released by their predator, a midge larva. The spines lower a flea's risk of being eaten but slow its reproduction. Researchers collected fleas from a lake where midge larvae had been absent for several decades and exposed them to midge chemicals in the laboratory. These fleas grew spines just as readily as fleas taken from lakes where midges were common, which suggests that ______

passages.title: Shade trees
passages.text:
A city planted trees along some streets in 2019 to reduce summer heat. A researcher compared average midday street-surface temperatures in July.
Streets with new trees: 41°C in 2018; 38°C in 2023.
Streets without new trees: 40°C in 2018; 40°C in 2023.
The researcher concludes that the trees, rather than a citywide change in weather, most likely explain the cooling on the planted streets.

passages.title: Dating a map
passages.text: The museum's oldest map was long thought to date from the early ______ recent analysis of its paper, however, suggests that it was drawn more than a century later.

passages.title: Saturn's rings
passages.text: For two centuries after their discovery, many astronomers assumed that Saturn's rings were solid sheets of material. In the 1850s, the physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed mathematically that a solid ring of that size would be torn apart by Saturn's gravity. ______ he argued, the rings must consist of countless separate particles, each orbiting the planet on its own.

passages.title: Tree rings and a shipwreck
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Divers found the wreck of a wooden ship in the Baltic Sea.
- Radiocarbon dating of the wood gave a possible range of about 150 years.
- Each year's weather affects how wide a tree's growth ring is, so a sequence of rings forms a pattern unique to those years.
- Researchers matched the ring pattern in the ship's oak planks to a regional record of tree-ring widths.
- The match showed that the trees were cut down in the winter of 1611-1612.

passages.title: A mixed review
passages.text: The critic's praise for the new film was ______: although she admired its cinematography, she devoted most of her review to faulting the script, the pacing, and the lead performance.

passages.title: Marigolds and nematodes
passages.text: Farmers have long noticed that tomato plants grown beside marigolds suffer less damage from root-knot nematodes, tiny worms that attack roots. One explanation is that marigold roots release a compound that is toxic to the nematodes; another is that marigolds encourage the growth of soil fungi that prey on nematodes. To test these ideas, researchers sterilized a batch of soil, killing any fungi, and then added equal numbers of nematodes to sterilized and unsterilized pots, each containing a tomato plant beside a marigold. Nematode numbers ended up just as low in the sterilized pots as in the unsterilized ones, and both were far lower than in comparison pots without marigolds, which suggests that ______

passages.title: A reading app
passages.text:
A school district gave a reading app to some students in grades 4 and 5 and compared their gains on a spring reading test with the gains of students who did not use the app.
Students who began the year below grade level: app users gained 14 points; nonusers gained 6 points.
Students who began the year at grade level: app users gained 9 points; nonusers gained 5 points.
A district analyst concludes that the app benefited students who began below grade level more than it benefited students who began at grade level.

passages.title: Why a dialect fades
passages.text:
Text 1
In the valleys of one mountain region, younger residents use far fewer of the region's traditional dialect features than their grandparents do. A linguist attributes the change to television, arguing that decades of exposure to broadcast speech have pulled local speakers toward a national standard.

Text 2
Sociolinguist Mara Vint interviewed residents of the same region who reported watching similar amounts of television. Those who had spent several years working in distant cities had dropped most dialect features, while those who had always lived in the valleys still used them heavily. Vint argues that face-to-face contact with speakers of other varieties, not broadcast speech, reshapes how people talk.

passages.title: The order slip
passages.text: Mrs. Avery had kept the bookshop for thirty years and prided herself on finding any book a customer could name. When a young man came in asking for a novel she had never heard of, she smiled and promised to order it. After he left, she wrote the title on a slip of paper, studied it for a long moment, and then tucked it into the drawer where she kept the letters she did not intend to answer.

passages.title: Newton's telescope
passages.text: Early telescopes surrounded their images with fringes of false color, because their glass lenses bent different colors of light by different amounts. Isaac Newton concluded, wrongly as it turned out, that no arrangement of lenses could ever remove this flaw. ______ he built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror, which reflects all colors equally.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: several of the letters she herself cites show delegates on the verge of abandoning the talks
candidates.explanation: Her own sources show the talks nearly collapsed, so the claim that agreement was inevitable is not supported by the evidence: it is "unwarranted."

A.rationale: "Exhaustive" describes thorough research, which the text grants; the problem is with the conclusion's support.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the conclusion was copied from other historians.

D.rationale: An inevitable outcome is a strong claim, not an understated one.

hints: What do her own sources show about the talks?
candidates.remember: When a text says a conclusion conflicts with its own evidence, look for "unsupported."

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: growing spines is costly enough that the fleas living in lakes without any midges have gradually lost the ability to grow them.
choices.B: midge larvae have recently returned to the lake from which the researchers collected the fleas.
choices.C: the fleas' ability to grow spines in response to the predator has lasted through decades without it.
choices.D: fleas in lakes with midges reproduce more quickly than fleas in lakes where midges are absent.

candidates.evidence: These fleas grew spines just as readily
candidates.explanation: Fleas from a lake without midges for decades still grew spines when exposed to midge chemicals, so the ability has lasted without recent exposure.

A.rationale: The fleas from the midge-free lake grew spines just as readily, so they had not lost the ability.

B.rationale: The text says only that the midges had been absent; nothing indicates their return.

D.rationale: The study compared spine growth, not reproduction rates in the wild.

hints: What did the fleas from the midge-free lake do?

strategy.explanation: State the result, then choose the conclusion it directly supports.

candidates.remember: An inference must follow from the result itself, not from outside assumptions.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: quantitative (isolating a cause)
candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the researcher's conclusion?

choices.A: Planted streets cooled from 41°C to 38°C, while unplanted streets stayed at 40°C over the same period.
choices.B: Streets with new trees had an average midday temperature of 38°C in 2023, which was 3 degrees lower than in 2018.
choices.C: In 2023, streets with new trees were on average 2 degrees cooler at midday than streets without new trees were.
choices.D: In 2018, before any trees were planted, streets that later received trees were warmer than streets that did not.

candidates.evidence: rather than a citywide change in weather
candidates.explanation: A citywide weather change would have cooled all streets. Only A shows that the unplanted streets did not cool while the planted ones did.

B.rationale: This shows cooling on the planted streets but not that unplanted streets failed to cool, so it cannot rule out a weather change.

C.rationale: A one-year comparison ignores that the planted streets started out warmer; it does not show a change over time.

D.rationale: This describes the starting point only and says nothing about what changed.

hints: What would the data show if weather caused the cooling?

strategy.explanation: Ask what comparison rules out the alternative.

candidates.remember: To rule out a general cause, show that the comparison group did not change.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: recent analysis of its paper, however, suggests
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined, and "however" sits inside the second clause, not at the boundary. A semicolon is needed between the clauses.

A.rationale: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; "however" is not a conjunction.

B.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

C.rationale: A colon introduces an explanation or elaboration, but the second clause contradicts the first.

hints: Where does the first independent clause end?

strategy.explanation: Find the two clauses, then ignore "however" when choosing the boundary.

candidates.remember: A mid-clause "however" does not join clauses; the boundary still needs a semicolon or period.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: would be torn apart by Saturn's gravity
candidates.explanation: Maxwell rejected the solid-ring view and proposed particles in its place, so "Instead" fits.

A.rationale: Maxwell's conclusion replaces the solid-ring idea; it does not resemble it.

C.rationale: The particle model is not an example of a solid ring being torn apart.

D.rationale: "Nonetheless" would mean he argued for particles despite his own result, but the result is the reason.

hints: Does the last sentence replace, support, or contrast with the earlier idea?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use "instead" when one explanation replaces another.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why the researchers' method produced a more precise date than radiocarbon dating did. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Researchers matched the ring pattern in the ship's oak planks to a regional record of tree-ring widths, and the trees turned out to have been cut in 1611-1612.
choices.B: Radiocarbon dating of the wood from the Baltic Sea shipwreck gave a range of about 150 years, which made it hard for researchers to say when the ship was built.
choices.C: Since ring widths vary with each year's weather, matching the planks to a regional record narrowed the date to one winter, not a 150-year range.
choices.D: The trees used to build the Baltic Sea ship were cut down in the winter of 1611-1612, a date found by comparing tree rings.

candidates.evidence: Each year's weather affects how wide a tree's growth ring is
candidates.explanation: Only C gives the reason the method is precise (each year's weather leaves a distinctive ring) and contrasts the result (one winter) with radiocarbon's 150-year range.

A.rationale: This reports the method and the date but does not explain why the method was more precise than radiocarbon dating.

B.rationale: This describes radiocarbon's limitation but not why the other method did better.

D.rationale: This gives the date but neither compares it with radiocarbon dating nor explains the method's precision.

hints: Which choice says why the method worked better?

strategy.explanation: Look for a reason and a comparison.

candidates.remember: When the goal says "why," the answer must give a reason, not just a result.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.explanation: Her praise covered only the cinematography and was outweighed by criticism, so it was "qualified," meaning limited or held back by reservations.

A.rationale: "Effusive" means gushing, but her praise is limited to one feature and outweighed by criticism.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the critic hid her identity.

D.rationale: Nothing concerns when the review appeared relative to the film.

hints: How much of the review is praise?
candidates.remember: Read past the colon: it tells you how far the praise went.

revision_history.reason: solvers: double negative "hardly unreserved" fits a mostly negative review awkwardly; rebuilt as "qualified" praise with new options

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the marigolds' effect on the nematodes does not depend on soil fungi.
choices.B: soil fungi that prey on nematodes are more common near marigolds than near tomato plants.
choices.C: compounds released by marigold roots are harmful to tomato plants as well as to nematodes.
choices.D: sterilizing soil reduces nematode numbers even when no marigolds are present.

candidates.evidence: Nematode numbers ended up just as low in the sterilized pots
candidates.explanation: Removing the fungi did not change the result, so the fungi cannot be what lowers nematode numbers; the effect works without them, which leaves the root-compound explanation standing.

B.rationale: The experiment did not measure where fungi are common; it removed them and found no change.

C.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns harm to the tomato plants.

D.rationale: No pots without marigolds were tested, and nematodes were added after sterilizing.

hints: What changed between the two kinds of pots, and did the outcome change?

strategy.explanation: Identify the variable the experiment removed.

candidates.remember: If removing a factor changes nothing, that factor is not the cause.

revision_history.reason: solvers: "just as low" lacked a marigold-free baseline; passage now states both were far lower than pots without marigolds

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the analyst's conclusion?

choices.A: Below-grade app users gained 14 points over the school year, a larger gain than that of any other group of students in the comparison.
choices.B: At-grade students who used the app gained 9 points, compared with 5 points for at-grade students who did not.
choices.C: In both groups, students who used the app gained more points over the year than students in the same group who did not use the app.
choices.D: Below-grade users gained 8 more points than below-grade nonusers, but at-grade users gained only 4 more than at-grade nonusers.

candidates.evidence: benefited students who began below grade level more
candidates.explanation: The app's benefit in each group is the difference between users and nonusers: 14 - 6 = 8 for below-grade students and 9 - 5 = 4 for at-grade students. Only D compares these two differences.

A.rationale: A large gain alone does not show the app's benefit, which requires comparison with nonusers in the same group.

B.rationale: This shows a benefit for only one group and cannot show which group benefited more.

C.rationale: This shows the app helped both groups but not that it helped one group more.

hints: How do you measure the app's benefit within one group?

strategy.explanation: Compute the user-minus-nonuser difference for each group, then compare.

candidates.remember: "Benefited more" compares two differences, not two raw scores.

revision_history.reason: solver: key slightly longest and only computed option; key shortened

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Vint (Text 2) most likely respond to the linguist's explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: She would agree that television is the main cause but add that spending years working in distant cities speeds up the loss of dialect features.
choices.B: She would argue that because residents with similar television viewing differed in dialect use, television is unlikely to explain the change.
choices.C: She would dispute that younger residents use fewer dialect features than older residents do.
choices.D: She would argue that watching television makes residents more likely to keep traditional dialect features.

candidates.evidence: who reported watching similar amounts of television
candidates.explanation: Vint compared people with similar television viewing and found a large difference tied to living in cities, so she would say television cannot account for the difference and that face-to-face contact does.

A.rationale: Vint's data hold television roughly constant and still find a difference, so she does not grant that television is the main cause.

C.rationale: Vint does not question the decline; she questions its cause.

D.rationale: Vint draws no conclusion that television preserves the dialect.

hints: What did Vint hold constant in her comparison?

strategy.explanation: Find the factor that was the same in both groups she compared.

candidates.remember: If a factor is held equal and outcomes still differ, it is not the explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It reveals that Mrs. Avery's bookshop is struggling to pay the suppliers who send it books.
choices.B: It shows that Mrs. Avery has forgotten the title the young man asked for.
choices.C: It suggests that Mrs. Avery does not actually mean to order the book she promised.
choices.D: It indicates that Mrs. Avery plans to write to the young man about the novel.

candidates.evidence: the letters she did not intend to answer
candidates.explanation: Placing the order slip with letters she will never answer implies she will set the request aside, which undercuts the promise and her pride in finding any book.

A.rationale: The drawer holds letters she will not answer, not unpaid bills; nothing concerns the shop's finances.

B.rationale: She wrote the title down and studied it, so she has not forgotten it.

D.rationale: The drawer is for letters she does not intend to answer, which points the other way.

hints: What kind of things go in that drawer?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the drawer's contents imply about the slip.

candidates.remember: In literary texts, a detail often reveals what a character does not say.

revision_history.reason: solver: distractor A noticeably longest; shortened

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: no arrangement of lenses could ever remove this flaw
candidates.explanation: Because Newton believed lenses could not be fixed, he turned to a mirror; the action is a consequence of the belief, so "Accordingly" fits. The aside "wrongly as it turned out" does not change why he acted.

B.rationale: Building a mirror telescope follows from his conclusion; it does not go against it.

C.rationale: The mirror telescope is not an example of the conclusion that lenses cannot be fixed.

D.rationale: Nothing is being contrasted; the action is a response to the conclusion.

hints: Why did Newton build a mirror telescope?

strategy.explanation: Label the link between the second and third sentences.

candidates.remember: Ignore asides; ask how the action relates to the reasoning that led to it.

revision_history.reason: solver: aside may lure to Nevertheless; aside is the intended difficulty and the logic is unchanged; resubmitted for fresh blind solve unchanged
